text: The ticket says updating an incident now takes four to five seconds, with no further detail. This lab works it exactly the way lessons five through seven taught: measure first with the profiler, then fix exactly what the measurement points to — nothing more.

Debug business rule and debug script get switched on, and the exact save gets repeated. Two real suspects stand out: sync task owners takes twenty-four hundred milliseconds, almost all of it inside one script include method, and recalculate sla flag fires several times in a row with durations shrinking toward zero — the exact two signatures from lessons six and seven, both showing up in the same transaction.

Inside that script include, for every task linked to the incident, the code opens a brand-new GlideRecord against sys_user and queries it one task at a time. Forty linked tasks means forty separate user lookups — the repeated-query signature, just against a different table than the examples so far.

The fix collects the distinct user IDs actually needed, runs one query with an IN condition against all of them, and reads the names back out of a plain lookup map keyed by user ID. Forty queries become one, and the result is identical.

Recalculate SLA flag turns out to be the other pattern exactly: an after business rule that calls current dot update to save its own computed field, re-triggering update business rules on the same table. The fix is the same combination from lesson seven — skip the save entirely when the value hasn't actually changed, and call setWorkflow false right before the save that remains, so it can't re-trigger business rules at all.

Four steps, start to finish: profile the exact slow transaction to find real suspects instead of guessing; fix the query stuck inside the loop with a lookup map; fix the business rule that fires repeatedly with a guard and setWorkflow false; and re-run the same profiler afterward to confirm both fixes actually worked, not just assume they did.

With both fixes confirmed and the transaction back under half a second, this chapter on diagnosing slow scripts is done. Chapter three moves one level deeper, into the database itself, starting with lesson nine: indexes on the platform.
